CNN: What comes next after Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal charges
CNBC: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty in federal case for UnitedHealthcare CEO killing
NPR: Mangione pleads guilty in federal court, leaving fate of state trial uncertain
NBC News: Judge delays Luigi Mangione's state murder trial after double jeopardy claim
Altoona Mirror: Timeline of Mangione's criminal cases

CBS New York: Newly unsealed footage shows Luigi Mangione's arrest in Pennsylvania

content.p: On Friday 14 August 2026, Luigi Mangione stood in a federal courtroom in Manhattan and described the killing publicly in his own words for the first time, according to CNN. "I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan, and he died," he told Judge Margaret Garnett. "I knew what I was doing was illegal." He was pleading guilty to two federal stalking counts connected to the killing of Brian Thompson, the chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, who had been shot on a midtown sidewalk on 4 December 2024.

The plea ended one of the two main prosecutions against him, and it opened a harder legal question. Within hours his lawyers asked a New York state judge to throw out the state murder case, arguing that New York's double jeopardy law forbids prosecuting him a second time for the same event. He has pleaded not guilty to the state charges, and he is presumed innocent of them unless a jury convicts him. As of early October 2026 the double jeopardy motion was undecided, and the federal sentencing was set for 18 December.

Thompson was 50 and the father of two. According to the Altoona Mirror's timeline, he reached New York on 2 December 2024 and stayed at a hotel across the street from the New York Hilton Midtown, where UnitedHealth Group's annual investor conference was to be held. On the morning of 4 December he was walking to the conference when he was shot outside the Hilton. NPR described him as alone on the street, hours before he was due to host the event.

Prosecutors say a man they identify as Mangione had arrived in the city on a Greyhound bus on 24 November. They say he checked into a hostel using a fake New Jersey driver's license in the name Mark Rosario. On the day of the shooting, the same account says, the gunman waited in the area for about an hour before ambushing Thompson, then fled through Central Park to upper Manhattan, took the subway to Penn Station and boarded an Amtrak train to Philadelphia, according to police. Surveillance video captured the shooting.

Police released images of the suspect the next day, including one showing his face at the hostel. On 6 December they found a backpack in Central Park that they said the shooter had discarded; it held Monopoly money and a black Tommy Hilfiger jacket.

On 9 December 2024, five days after the shooting, police in Altoona, Pennsylvania, were sent to a McDonald's on Plank Road after a report of a man who resembled the suspect. CNBC reported that a person recognised him from a surveillance photo. According to the timeline, the man gave officers the Mark Rosario name and a fake ID before identifying himself as Luigi Mangione, and he was arrested.

CBS New York, which obtained newly unsealed body camera footage in October 2026, reported that officers questioned him about the fake license and that he later told them he "shouldn't have" lied about who he was. Police searched his backpack, and CNN reported that authorities said it held a gun tying him to the scene, plus a notebook. The timeline describes the weapon as a 3D-printed pistol that prosecutors say matches the one used to kill Thompson, and the notebook as describing a wish to "wack" a health insurance executive. CNN quoted notebook writings about targeting the CEO at the "parasitic bean-counter convention."

The footage had been played at a three-week evidentiary hearing that began in December 2025, when defence lawyers argued the backpack search violated Mangione's rights. News organisations, ABC News among them, petitioned the court, and the full video, including a redacted version of a strip search at the Altoona police station, was released on Friday 2 October 2026. In May 2026, according to the timeline, Judge Gregory Carro ruled that prosecutors could use the gun, notebook and other items found in the backpack, but barred items officers had taken from the bag before Mangione was in custody: a loaded gun magazine, a cellphone, a passport and a wallet.

Mangione faced cases in three places: federal court, New York state court and Pennsylvania. On 17 December 2024 Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg announced a state indictment including murder as an act of terrorism, calling the killing "a frightening, well-planned, targeted murder that was intended to cause shock and attention and intimidation." Two days later Mangione was extradited and flown to New York, where he was led along a Manhattan pier by armed officers in front of news cameras, and he was charged in federal court with stalking and murder.

He pleaded not guilty to the state charges on 23 December. His lawyer complained that the dueling prosecutions had turned him into a "human ping-pong ball." From the start the defence argued he was being tried twice for one crime. Judge Carro had earlier called the argument premature while the federal case remained open.

On 1 April the then US Attorney General, Pam Bondi, said she had directed federal prosecutors to seek the death penalty, calling the killing "an act of political violence." Mangione pleaded not guilty to a federal murder charge on 25 April as prosecutors formally declared that intent.

The state case changed shape in September, when Judge Carro threw out the terrorism counts, rejecting the theory that the killing was "intended to evoke terror." That removed the top two charges and the possibility of a mandatory sentence of life without parole, the timeline says. CNN reported that the original indictment had 11 counts and that the judge dismissed those two plus a weapons charge. Second-degree murder stayed, and it can carry a life sentence.

On 30 January 2026 Judge Garnett barred federal prosecutors from seeking the death penalty, dismissing the federal murder charge that had allowed it, and ruled prosecutors could use evidence from the backpack. At a court appearance on 6 February Mangione himself objected to back-to-back trials: "It's the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any commonsense definition."

In June 2026, according to the timeline, Judge Carro disclosed that Mangione planned to claim extreme emotional disturbance at the state trial. The next day his lawyers reversed course and said they would not pursue a psychiatric defense.

The federal plea came at a conference scheduled in haste, hours after Mangione appeared in state court that week, CNN reported. CNN had also reported plea negotiations, but defence lawyers confirmed in court that no agreement was reached. US Attorney Jamie McDonald said at a news conference that Mangione chose to plead to the indictment with no incentive from a deal. His federal trial, which had been scheduled for January 2027, was therefore avoided.

NPR noted that Mangione arrived in what looked like tan prison fatigues rather than the suits he had worn to earlier hearings. He read a prepared statement quickly enough that the judge asked him to slow down. In it, he said that "after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back, navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system and witnessing similar experiences of countless others," he learned that UnitedHealthcare would hold its investor conference in New York on 4 December 2024, though the location had not been made public.

He said he emailed the company's leadership, posing as an investor at a firm managing more than $50 billion in assets, to ask about the conference, and got an answer within an hour. "Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour," he said. He added that he used a 3D printer to make part of a gun and equipped it with a silencer and magazine before travelling to New York. "My travel to New York and email to United Healthcare was with the intent to shoot Brian Thompson." CNN and NPR reported that he voiced no remorse.

Prosecutors described their evidence in court, including security footage. NPR reported that they cited an overwhelming amount of evidence, including DNA and fingerprints from the scene. Thompson's mother, widow and other relatives were visibly emotional during the hearing.

Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Mangione's lawyer, said Mangione had "accepted full responsibility for the death of Brian Thompson." She said he "believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life." Thompson's family called the plea "an important step toward justice" and asked the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of the crime. They also noted that proceedings in New York and Pennsylvania were still to come.

US Attorney McDonald said Mangione had admitted to stalking and murdering Thompson "in broad daylight" and that "no grievance, political belief, or ideological cause can justify murder." New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch called the day "an important moment of accountability." UnitedHealth Group said Thompson's life "was cut short by an act of violence that devastated everyone who knew and loved him."

NPR noted that elected officials across the political spectrum condemned politically motivated violence, but that Mangione had won strong public support, with many viewing him as a vigilante against an unfair health care system. It said supporters had donated more than $1.5 million to his defence fund, according to a website run by pro-Mangione volunteers. CNN noted that fewer protesters and onlookers gathered outside the court than at earlier hearings.

Judge Garnett told Mangione he faces a maximum of life in prison. Prosecutors told the court that sentencing guidelines suggest about 24 to 30 years, but the judge is not bound by them. Because there is no plea deal, there is no agreed sentencing range. McDonald said his office will seek life. Former federal prosecutor Berit Berger told CNN it is "very likely" the sentence will be life or close to it, and noted that the judge may consider all of the conduct that day and in the days around it, not only the stalking counts.

The defence filed its motion immediately after the plea, asking Judge Carro to dismiss the second-degree murder and weapons counts. That covers seven of the eight remaining state charges. The one it left out is the forged-instrument charge over the fake identification, which the motion says happened on a different date and at a different place. The motion also accused state and federal prosecutors of coordinating so the state trial would go first, in order to "avoid double jeopardy protections," and of having "sensationalized this case." The Manhattan District Attorney's office said it was "prepared to litigate the defense motions."

New York's statute goes further than the US Constitution, CNN's legal analysts explained: it bars separate prosecutions for different offences arising from the same criminal transaction. Former prosecutor Anthony Capozzolo told CNN it was "more likely than not that the state case goes away." New York criminal defense attorney Stacy Schneider called the defence argument a "calculated, good shot" but "not a slam dunk," and said prosecutors would likely argue that stalking was a prelude to the murder, not the act of pulling the trigger. NPR noted that if the state trial proceeds, prosecutors could use his admission against him.

On 17 August Judge Carro postponed the trial, which had been due to start on 8 September. He gave prosecutors until 9 October to respond and the defence until 30 October to reply, and set the next court date for 10 December. NBC News quoted a source who said the District Attorney's office intended to fight the motion until it sees the federal sentence. CNN reported that if the office is satisfied with that sentence, it could agree to dismiss the state charges. Either side could appeal Carro's ruling. CBS reported in October that a decision on whether the state case goes ahead was still pending.
